title: What inflation does the RBI actually fight?
tension: There is a strange split at the heart of how India runs monetary policy. The number the RBI is legally told to target, headline CPI, is dominated by food and fuel, the two things its interest rates are least able to control. So economists watch a second, quieter number, core inflation, that strips food and fuel out to see the underlying trend. The result is an awkward truth: the inflation the RBI fights with the repo rate is often not the inflation that is actually hurting you at the vegetable cart.
teachingGoal: Teach the core-versus-headline distinction and why it matters for policy: what core inflation is and why food and fuel are stripped out, how core and headline can diverge, why the RBI targets headline by law but leans on core to read the trend, the 4% target and tolerance band, and how the repo rate is the lever. The reader should understand why the official target and their lived inflation can be two different things.
sectionArc: Headline versus core: what is the difference? (headline CPI is the all-items number; core strips out food and fuel; today's core and headline rates side by side)
Why strip out food and fuel at all? (they are volatile and supply-driven; their swings can hide or exaggerate the underlying trend; core is meant to show the 'sticky' inflation beneath the noise)
When core and headline disagree, who is right? (both; they answer different questions; a spike in onions lifts headline but not core, a broad rise in services lifts core; show the gap)
So which one does the RBI target? (by law, headline CPI at 4% within a 2-6% band; but it watches core closely to judge whether inflation is becoming entrenched)

Right now the two split sharply: what should the RBI do? (headline near 1%, below the 4% target, because food prices are falling, while core sits up around 4.6%; the live dilemma, cut rates to support growth because headline is soft, or hold because underlying inflation is still sticky)
How does the repo rate even work on prices? (raising the policy rate makes borrowing dearer, cools demand, and is meant to pull inflation down, slowly and bluntly; today's repo rate)
Why is this a genuine dilemma? (the RBI is told to hit a number driven by food and fuel that its main tool barely touches; tighten too hard for a food spike and you choke the economy for nothing)
So what should you take from core versus headline? (headline is your cost of living; core is the trend the RBI steers by; watching both tells you whether a price rise is a blip or a tide)
mustTeach: headline CPI is the all-items inflation rate; core inflation excludes the volatile food and fuel components
food and fuel are stripped out because they are volatile and largely supply-driven, obscuring the underlying trend
core and headline can diverge sharply, and each answers a different question
the RBI's legal target is headline CPI at 4% (2-6% band), but it leans on core to judge whether inflation is entrenched
the policy repo rate is the RBI's main lever, working slowly and bluntly by cooling demand
interest rates are weak against the food and fuel that dominate headline, which is the core-vs-headline dilemma

CURRENCY (important): the current official basket is the 2024-base series, launched 12 Feb 2026. Use the 2024 weights (food and beverages 36.75%) as the CURRENT weights, and cite the old 2012 weights only to show what changed. The detailed month-by-month component inflation figures (vegetables, onion, etc.) come from the longer 2012-base series and must be framed as recent readings under the previous basket, never invented for the new base.

contextCards.fact: Core inflation strips out food and fuel from the headline index. The point is not that food and fuel do not matter (they matter enormously to households), but that they are volatile and supply-driven, so their swings can mask the slower, more persistent inflation in everything else. Central banks watch core to judge whether inflation is becoming entrenched, because that 'sticky' inflation is what interest rates can actually influence.
contextCards.source: Standard central-banking practice on core inflation (uncontested)

contextCards.fact: Under the 2016 framework the RBI's legal target is headline CPI inflation at 4 percent, within a tolerance band of 2 to 6 percent, set by a six-member Monetary Policy Committee. Its main instrument is the policy repo rate, the rate at which it lends to banks: raising it makes credit costlier and cools demand, lowering it does the reverse. The tool works on demand, slowly, which is why it is poorly suited to supply-driven food and fuel spikes.
contextCards.source: RBI flexible inflation-targeting framework (2016); Monetary Policy Committee (verified)

contextCards.fact: On 12 February 2026 India launched a new Consumer Price Index series with base year 2024 (replacing 2012), built on the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey of 2023-24. The biggest change: the weight of food and beverages fell from 45.86% to 36.75%, because Indians now spend a smaller share of their budgets on food and more on services, a textbook case of Engel's law. Housing and utilities rose to about 17.7%, transport and communication to about 12.4%, and health to about 6.1%. The basket grew from 299 to 358 items, adding e-commerce and online prices, telecom data plans and OTT streaming subscriptions for the first time, and switched to the international COICOP classification of 12 divisions instead of the old six groups. Headline inflation on the new base was 2.75% in January 2026.
contextCards.source: MoSPI / NSO, first CPI release on base 2024=100, 12 February 2026; HCES 2023-24
